transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Polar Labs CTO), Nina Reyes (Platform Lead), Samir Patel (SRE), Olivia Chen (Security)

[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. Maya is our SE. quick agenda, we'll run through token routing and tenant siloing patterns, show the console, then talk pilot.

[00:22] Ethan Cole: thanks, Jordan. To set context, Polar's building a multi-tenant inference layer for internal apps and a couple external partners. Primary concerns are latency variability, noisy tenants, and cost controls. We want to see how org/project keys map to policies.

[00:45] Maya Singh: perfect. we'll start high level — two primitives we use: org keys (global identity for billing/owner) and project keys (scoped tokens for apps or teams). routing policies can attach to either key level to do priority lanes, quota slices, and sticky routing.

[01:10] Nina Reyes: quick question, is project key an API key or a namespace concept? how do we map it to our auth?

[01:18] Maya Singh: it's an API key; you can mint project keys under an org. they inherit org-level billing but you can attach different quotas, concurrency caps, and routing weights. Many customers integrate with their own key minting from CI/CD or internal auth, or use our CRL. there is SSO mapping as well for console access.

[01:44] Samir Patel: can we enforce per-project burst windows? some teams have spiky jobs. we want to prevent noisy bursts from taking down critical flows.

[01:52] Maya Singh: yes — we demo two mechanisms: rate slices (time-windowed quotas per project) and fairburst which gives transient credit that drains under pressure. you can also set sticky routing so certain keys always route to a reserved pool for SLAs.

[02:20] Jordan Park: i'll share my screen and open the console.

[02:35] [screen share starts]

[02:38] Jordan Park: welcome to the org view. here you can see org-level throughput, token spend, and active keys. on the right is the routing policy editor — we're showing a sample policy that maps high-priority project keys to a dedicated lane backed by dedicated capacity. low priority keys are routed to a cost-optimized quantized variant.

[03:05] Ethan Cole: is that quantized variant pinned to the same model but q4 / int8? we have accuracy-sensitive partners who won't accept heavy quant.

[03:16] Maya Singh: correct, you can pin a model variant per lane. for accuracy-sensitive keys you pin to fp16 or tuned non-quantized. the fallback chain will only pick cheaper variants when the dedicated lane is at capacity and the policy allows degrading.

[03:44] [04:00] Speaker 1: oh can you show the api example, how would an application switch keys?

[04:06] Maya Singh: sure — a simple header x-api-key is used. we published SDK examples. here's a curl that posts to /v1/generate with project-key; the billing shows up under org but usage attributed to project.

[04:28] Jordan Park: now i'd like to highlight quota slicing. imagine you have a 1M token monthly allotment for an org; we let you carve that into per-project monthly, daily, and concurrency quotas.

[04:43] Nina Reyes: is concurrency measured in in-flight requests or tokens/sec?

[04:48] Maya Singh: in-flight requests per assigned capacity shard. tokens are separate metering units. concurrency limits are the simplest way to prevent noisy tenants from taking GPU slots.

[05:05] Ethan Cole: what about backpressure — if a lane is full, do we drop or enqueue?

[05:10] Maya Singh: configurable. default is immediate 429 with descriptive retry-after. you can enable queueing with estimated wait and automatic fallback to a best-effort lane, or you can implement a leaky bucket style smoothing policy.

[05:40] Jordan Park: i'll flip to the API throttling page — here you can define per-key rate windows, hard caps, and allow bursts up to X. we also provide usage alerts.

[05:55] Samir Patel: any observability hooks for tracing tokens across services? we want to correlate a degraded response to specific project key activity.

[06:03] Maya Singh: yes — token-level traces are emitted and you can forward spans into your tracing system. console shows per-key latency pctls, error rates, and cost. we also export logs for audit.

[06:30] Olivia Chen: security quick note — we need audit logs retention, KMS integration for key material, SSO + RBAC for minting keys. do you support customer-managed keys and on-prem private control plane?

[06:45] Maya Singh: we do. Redwood Private supports VPC deployment and customer-managed KMS/HSM. audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM and we have SOC2 + ISO attestation — i'll follow up with docs.

[07:05] Jordan Park: demo time — routing policy editor live change. switching this project key from shared to reserved lane. we'll apply and show simulated requests.

[07:20] [08:00] ambient typing and short delay

[08:04] Maya Singh: simulation shows 95th latency goes from 340ms to 120ms for that key when moved to reserved lane. concurrent cost goes up but predictable.

[08:20] Ethan Cole: that difference is compelling. what's the minimum committed capacity for a reserved lane?

[08:29] Jordan Park: typical reserved pools start at 4 GPUs for moderate throughput, but we can do flexible commits. pricing sheet will show options.

[08:44] Nina Reyes: how do we handle cross-region routing? some of our customers need EU residency.

[08:51] Maya Singh: routing policies include region affinity; you can pin keys to regions and have fallback policies. for data residency you'll want Private or Dedicated with region-specific capacity.

[09:15] Samir Patel: we generate synchronous user-facing responses and async batch jobs. can a project key be limited to certain endpoints (e.g., embeddings only)?

[09:24] Maya Singh: yes, you can apply per-route quotas and method-level RBAC so a key can be allowed embeddings but blocked from generation or have tighter limits.

[09:44] Jordan Park: switching to billing controls — we have org-level soft budgets that trigger throttles or warnings when crossed. you can configure alerts at project granularity.

[10:02] Olivia Chen: can we export invoicing per-project for chargeback?

[10:07] Jordan Park: absolutely, invoice breakdowns by project are available and can be exported as CSV.

[10:20] [10:30] Ethan Cole: let's talk pilot scope. we want to run a 30-day pilot with two project keys: one reserved lane for our core product and one shared lane for non-critical tooling. goals: stable p95 latency under 250ms for core, plus validate quota enforcement.

[10:46] Maya Singh: sounds good. recommended bench: run a mixed workload with synthetic user traffic plus a few heavy-burst backfills to exercise fairburst and backpressure. we'll provide load harness and sample scripts.

[11:10] Samir Patel: we'll need to mirror our production auth so switching keys is seamless. do you support key rotation without downtime?

[11:18] Maya Singh: yes — keys can be rolled and both old and new accepted for a short overlap window. automation hooks available.

[11:32] Nina Reyes: curious about KV cache comments earlier — how does cache affinity interact with routing?

[11:38] Maya Singh: good callout. KV cache is per-serving shard; a reserved lane has its own cache warmup. if you route a key to a different lane frequently you'll get cold cache penalties. so we recommend sticky routing for latency-sensitive workloads. transcription sometimes shows KV as K V cash in our exports.

[12:00] Jordan Park: moving on — security details and docs. Maya will share SOC2 summary, KMS integration guide, and network diagram.

[12:12] Olivia Chen: do you have a documented pen test cadence and shareable report?

[12:17] Maya Singh: yes, we have recent pen test reports and can provide an exec summary.

[12:28] [13:00] short pause, background noise

[13:12] Ethan Cole: a bit of pushback from our procurement — we'd prefer a model where we can dynamically scale reserved capacity up during predictable windows and pause outside them. is that supported?

[13:26] Jordan Park: we offer burst capacity on top of reserved pools and scheduled autoscaling windows. contracts can include burst cushions.

[13:40] Nina Reyes: on the console, can we script policy changes via API? we want infra-as-code for routing policies.

[13:48] Maya Singh: yes, all console actions have API equivalents and a Terraform provider is in GA.

[14:00] Jordan Park: time for a quick Q&A and recap.

[14:05] Samir Patel: do you log full request payloads by default? we need to avoid PII retention.

[14:12] Maya Singh: default is no customer payload retention. you can opt-in for longer retention for debugging, but OM policy and compliance allow redaction. Private deployments can fully avoid storing payloads.

[14:34] Ethan Cole: competitors question — how is Redwood different from NimbusAI's managed endpoints?

[14:42] Jordan Park: short answer: our focus is production economics and unified tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private. we expose richer routing primitives and more granular project-level controls.

[15:00] Nina Reyes: ok next steps?

[15:05] Jordan Park: we'll email pilot proposal and pricing. Maya will attach policy examples and SDK snippets. Olivia will get compliance docs. Samir to send traffic patterns. we'll aim to kick off Aug 10.

[15:22] Ethan Cole: sounds good thanks.

[15:25] [END]

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present (names / acronyms sometimes mis-transcribed), natural speech interjections, and brief overlapping crosstalk around 08:00–09:00.
